title: Unitary and semigroup representations
subtitle: G2 lecture 066000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Expanded, source-grounded mathematical companion: independent derivations, worked examples, vector MathTex, reusable diagrams. Spoken source unchanged.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 066000 · The problem and its setting
slides.lead: An ordered spectral gap permits a Sylvester equation to be solved by integrating decaying exponentials.
body: For interlaced but separated spectra, the differences do not all share a sign, so we need a different construction. We study a related construction that works when the spectra are separated but their differences may have either sign.

The key change is to use unitary groups: exponentials with an imaginary unit in the exponent. These produce oscillations rather than decay. Then a scalar Fourier multiplier will turn each oscillation back into the reciprocal of its spectral difference.
slides.takeaway: Unitary transport replaces decay when the spectral differences change sign.

slides.title: The Sylvester orbit
slides.lead: Let A and B be bounded self-adjoint operators on complex Hilbert spaces.
body: Let C be a bounded map from the space on which B acts into the space on which A acts. For each real time t, define an operator U of t by exponentiating i times t times A.

Define V of t using B the same way. Because the generators are self-adjoint, U and V are unitary: they preserve lengths and have their adjoints as inverses. Now transport C by applying U of t on the left and the inverse of V of t on the right. Call the result F of t.
slides.takeaway: Two unitary groups move the unknown map by conjugate left/right actions.

slides.title: Check the orbit in diagonal coordinates
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 066000 · Check the orbit in diagonal coordinates
slides.lead: Assume for the moment that A and B are diagonal, with real eigenvalues a and b in the corresponding positions.
body: On the matrix entry joining a to b, left unitary evolution multiplies by the exponential of i t a. Right inverse evolution multiplies by the exponential of negative i t b. The product is the exponential of i t times a minus b.

Each matrix coefficient therefore oscillates with frequency equal to its spectral difference. Different entries can oscillate clockwise or counterclockwise depending on the sign of the difference. Unlike the ordered semigroup, there is no single exponential decay envelope.
slides.takeaway: Each spectral coefficient oscillates with its eigenvalue difference.

slides.title: A scalar reciprocal multiplier
slides.lead: Reciprocal differences can be represented by an integrable Fourier kernel.
body: Assume A and B are bounded self-adjoint and every cross-spectral difference ω satisfies |ω|≥δ>0. There is an integrable scalar kernel whose Fourier transform agrees with 1/ω on this separated frequency set.
The reciprocal can then be applied to the operator-valued unitary orbit. The norm of the kernel, not the number of eigenvalues, controls the resulting inverse.
slides.takeaway: An L1 Fourier kernel reproduces reciprocal values outside the forbidden gap.

slides.title: Build the operator inverse
slides.lead: Return to the operator orbit of C.
body: Multiply it by mu of t and integrate over all real t. Call the resulting operator Y. In diagonal coordinates, the entry of Y joining eigenvalues a and b is the entry of C times the integral of mu of t times the exponential of i t times a minus b.

The multiplier property evaluates this integral as one divided by a minus b. Therefore the entry of Y is the entry of C divided by the spectral difference. We have reconstructed the unique entrywise Sylvester solution.
slides.takeaway: Integrating the unitary orbit constructs the Sylvester inverse.

slides.title: Why the infinite-dimensional argument needs care
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 066000 · Why the infinite-dimensional argument needs care
body: Both e^(itA) and e^(−itB) are unitary. Hence their left/right multiplication does not increase the operator norm of C. Taking the norm inside the Bochner integral bounds X by ||μδ||₁·||C||.
For the kernel used in this lecture, ||μδ||₁=π/(2δ). This gives a dimension-independent bound even when the spectral sets are interlaced.
slides.takeaway: Unitary factors preserve operator norms, so only the kernel L1 norm remains.

slides.title: How the semigroup and unitary methods differ
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 066000 · How the semigroup and unitary methods differ
slides.lead: Let us compare the two integral constructions.
body: When A is entirely above B by delta, the semigroup integrand decays as the exponential of negative delta times time. We integrate only over nonnegative times, and the mass of the scalar envelope is one over delta.

For general pairwise-separated spectra, some spectral differences are positive and others negative. A single decaying semigroup cannot treat them all. The unitary representation works with both signs by oscillating over all real times and inserting a Fourier multiplier. The multiplier's absolute mass produces pi over two delta.
slides.takeaway: Semigroup and Fourier solutions exploit distinct spectral geometry.

slides.title: An example with both signs
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 066000 · An example with both signs
slides.lead: Let A be diagonal with entries negative one and positive one, and B the one-dimensional zero operator.
body: Let C be the column with entries two and three. The spectral differences are negative one and positive one, so delta equals one. The Sylvester solution has entries negative two and positive three. For the first coefficient, the unitary orbit oscillates with frequency negative one; for the second, with frequency positive one.

The scalar multiplier returns negative one for the first reciprocal and positive one for the second, producing exactly the required signs. No single choice of positive-time exponential decay using the same orientation can handle both entries.
slides.takeaway: Interlaced spectra separate from zero without admitting one ordered cut.

slides.title: The generator viewpoint
body: The maps sending X to U of t X V of negative t form a one-parameter unitary group on the Hilbert space of Hilbert–Schmidt operators. Its generator is multiplication by i times the Sylvester operator. In that Hilbert–Schmidt setting, the entire spectral calculation can be understood as functional calculus for a self-adjoint generator.

In Hilbert–Schmidt norm, spectral coefficients can also be estimated directly by orthogonal summation. For now, reconstruct the derivative of the orbit, verify the opposite-frequency example, and derive the norm estimate from the integral's absolute majorant.
slides.takeaway: The Sylvester operator generates the entire transport orbit.

slides.title: The Fourier method in one derivation
slides.lead: An ordered gap allows a decaying semigroup; a pairwise gap permits oscillatory unitary transport.
body: Every spectral coefficient of e^(itA)Ce^(−itB) oscillates with frequency aᵢ−bⱼ. Choose an integrable scalar kernel whose Fourier multiplier equals 1/ω outside the gap, and integrate the orbit. The result divides each coefficient by its frequency difference.
Unitary invariance bounds the result by the kernel’s L1 norm, π/(2δ), with no dimension factor.
slides.takeaway: An analytic multiplier replaces scalar division for mixed-sign differences.
